---
title: "Ordered beta regression"
execute:
  warning: false
  message: false
---

We need a distribution that assigns positive probability to exact zero, positive density to values between zero and one, and positive probability to exact one. [**Ordered beta regression**](https://doi.org/10.1017/pan.2022.20) joins those three pieces in one model.

The basic idea is to imagine one location for each predictor combination. Two boundaries divide that location scale into a lower endpoint region, an interior region, and an upper endpoint region. Within the interior region, a beta distribution describes the observed slider value. We fit the same population formula to both MegaNegRaising sliders so we can compare how voice and subject relate to each recorded response.

Following our [link notation](link-functions.qmd), we call the predictor location
for row $i$ $\eta_i$. This symbol gives the sum of that row's predictor values
and coefficients a short name; it does not name another observed variable. Two ordered
**cutpoints**, \(\kappa_0<\kappa_1\), divide the location scale into regions
associated with zero, the open interval, and one. For an interior response, the
positive **precision** \(\phi\) controls how concentrated the beta density is
around its mean: larger precision means less interior spread at a fixed mean.

The logistic [CDF](../random-variables-and-distributions/cumulative-distribution-functions.qmd) supplies probabilities for the endpoint regions, while the beta [variance](../random-variables-and-distributions/variance-and-covariance.qmd) describes spread conditional on an interior response. Fitting uses [maximum likelihood](../statistical-inference/maximum-likelihood.qmd): the observed slider values remain fixed while coefficients, cutpoints, and precision vary.

We begin with an observed endpoint response, generalize its contribution to all
three regions, and then fit both slider responses.

This model combines the threshold logic from [ordinal regression](ordinal-regression.qmd) with the interior [beta distribution](../random-variables-and-distributions/beta-distribution.qmd). It adds a strong **shared location assumption**: one predictor value $\eta_i$ simultaneously moves zero use, one use, and the center of interior responses. Separate endpoint logits plus a beta regression would relax that restriction.

```{r}
#| label: load-meganegraising-ordered-beta
#| echo: true
mnr <- read.csv("data/meganegraising/meganegraising-balanced.csv")
mnr$voice <- factor(mnr$voice, levels = c("active", "passive"))
mnr$subject <- factor(mnr$subject, levels = c("first", "third"))
X <- model.matrix(~ voice * subject, mnr)
```

The first observed exact-zero neg-raising response supplies a concrete starting
point:

```{r}
#| label: ordered-beta-observed-zero
#| echo: true
observed_zero_index <- which(mnr$negraising == 0)[[1L]]
cbind(
  mnr[observed_zero_index, c("voice", "subject", "negraising")],
  X[observed_zero_index, , drop = FALSE]
)
```

For this row, the recorded value is \(y_i=0\). Its likelihood contribution is
the probability that the latent location falls in the lower endpoint region:

$$
p_{0i}=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
\qquad
\eta_i=\sum_j x_{ij}\beta_j.
$$

The sum defining \(\eta_i\) multiplies each displayed design-row entry by its
coefficient and adds the products. We now add the contributions needed for
interior values and exact ones.

For ordered cutpoints $\kappa_0<\kappa_1$ and $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=0)=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(0<Y_i<1)=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
$$

$$
\mathbb{P}(Y_i=1)=1-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i).
$$

Conditional on the interior,

$$
Y_i\sim\operatorname{Beta}(\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
\qquad \mu_i=F(\eta_i).
$$

Let

$$
p_{0i}=F(\kappa_0-\eta_i),
\qquad
p_{1i}=1-F(\kappa_1-\eta_i),
$$

and $p_{mi}=F(\kappa_1-\eta_i)-F(\kappa_0-\eta_i)$. The contribution of one observed response is

$$
f(y_i\mid\eta_i,\kappa_0,\kappa_1,\phi)
=
\begin{cases}
p_{0i}, & y_i=0,\\[4pt]
p_{mi}\,\operatorname{Beta}(y_i\mid\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi),
& 0<y_i<1,\\[4pt]
p_{1i}, & y_i=1.
\end{cases}
$$

For \(n\) rows, conditional independence lets us multiply these observed-row
contributions. Computation uses the equivalent sum of their logarithms:

$$
L(\boldsymbol\beta,\kappa_0,\kappa_1,\phi)
=
\prod_{i=1}^{n}
f(y_i\mid\eta_i,\kappa_0,\kappa_1,\phi),
\qquad
-\log L
=
-\sum_{i=1}^{n}\log f(y_i\mid\eta_i,\kappa_0,\kappa_1,\phi).
$$

The three regions form a valid distribution because

$$
p_{0i}
+p_{mi}\int_0^1
\operatorname{Beta}(y\mid\mu_i\phi,(1-\mu_i)\phi)\,dy
+p_{1i}
=p_{0i}+p_{mi}+p_{1i}=1.
$$

We use the logistic CDF \(F\) because it keeps the ordered probabilities between
zero and one and makes the location additive in log odds. Bounded support alone
would permit other CDFs. The precision $\phi$ controls interior beta variance at
fixed $\mu_i$; endpoint mass is controlled by the ordered-region probabilities.

## Deriving the score

The score shows which way each parameter must move to increase the observed-row
likelihood. Let

$$
a_{0i}=\kappa_0-\eta_i,
\qquad
a_{1i}=\kappa_1-\eta_i,
\qquad
p_{mi}=F(a_{1i})-F(a_{0i}),
$$

and write $f(a)=F(a)[1-F(a)]$ for the logistic density. For a zero response,

$$
\frac{\partial\log p_{0i}}{\partial\eta_i}
=-[1-F(a_{0i})],
\qquad
\frac{\partial\log p_{0i}}{\partial\kappa_0}
=1-F(a_{0i}).
$$

For a one response,

$$
\frac{\partial\log p_{1i}}{\partial\eta_i}
=F(a_{1i}),
\qquad
\frac{\partial\log p_{1i}}{\partial\kappa_1}
=-F(a_{1i}).
$$

For an interior response, the region-probability part contributes

$$
\frac{\partial\log p_{mi}}{\partial\eta_i}
=
\frac{f(a_{0i})-f(a_{1i})}{p_{mi}},
$$

$$
\frac{\partial\log p_{mi}}{\partial\kappa_0}
=-\frac{f(a_{0i})}{p_{mi}},
\qquad
\frac{\partial\log p_{mi}}{\partial\kappa_1}
=\frac{f(a_{1i})}{p_{mi}}.
$$

The beta-density part also changes with $\eta_i$ and $\phi$. Set
$\alpha_i=\mu_i\phi$, $\beta_i=(1-\mu_i)\phi$, and let
$\psi$ denote the [digamma function](negative-binomial-regression.qmd), the
derivative of $\log\Gamma$. Differentiating the beta log density gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{\partial\log b(y_i;\alpha_i,\beta_i)}{\partial\eta_i}
&=
\mu_i(1-\mu_i)\phi
\left[
-\psi(\alpha_i)+\psi(\beta_i)
+\log y_i-\log(1-y_i)
\right],\\[4pt]
\frac{\partial\log b(y_i;\alpha_i,\beta_i)}{\partial\phi}
&=
\psi(\phi)
-\mu_i\psi(\alpha_i)
-(1-\mu_i)\psi(\beta_i)\\
&\quad
+\mu_i\log y_i
+(1-\mu_i)\log(1-y_i).
\end{aligned}
$$

The interior location score is the sum of its region and beta-density
contributions. Since $\eta_i=\mathbf x_i^\mathsf T\boldsymbol\beta$, the
coefficient score is $\mathbf X^\mathsf T\mathbf s_\eta$. Summing the cutpoint
and precision contributions gives their scores. The observed Hessian is the
derivative of this full score vector; its off-diagonal entries record, for
instance, how changing a coefficient changes the cutpoint score. We evaluate
that derivative numerically below and check it with a second numerical
calculation.

The visible likelihood below constrains the cutpoint gap and precision to be positive.

We must search for the coefficient, cutpoint, and precision values together.
Recall that a [derivative is a local rate of
change](../random-variables-and-distributions/expected-values.qmd#derivatives-as-local-rates-of-change).
A **gradient** collects that rate for every parameter of the negative log
likelihood. A **Hessian** collects the second derivatives and describes its local
curvature; the [Hessian](../statistical-inference/beyond-conjugacy.qmd#hessian-as-local-curvature)
develops that interpretation. We use **BFGS**, which builds an approximation to
the inverse Hessian from successive gradients and uses it to choose each next
parameter vector. Because we do not supply an analytic gradient to `optim()`, R
approximates each derivative by changing one parameter a small amount and
re-evaluating the negative log likelihood. The search ends when relative progress falls below `reltol`
or after `maxit` iterations.

After BFGS reaches the neighborhood of the optimum, we use the analytic score
derived above for four Newton updates. If $\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is the
gradient of the negative log likelihood and $\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta)$ is
its Hessian, one update solves

$$
\mathbf H(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})\boldsymbol\delta^{(t)}
=
\mathbf g(\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)})
$$

and sets

$$
\boldsymbol\theta^{(t+1)}
=
\boldsymbol\theta^{(t)}-\boldsymbol\delta^{(t)}.
$$

This step does not define another estimator. It tightens the same stationary
condition by using the local curvature after BFGS has already found the relevant
basin.

For parameter $\theta_j$, the central finite difference used in our independent
check is

$$
\frac{\partial\mathcal L}{\partial\theta_j}
\approx
\frac{
\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\theta+h\mathbf e_j)
-\mathcal L(\boldsymbol\theta-h\mathbf e_j)
}{2h},
$$

where $\mathbf e_j$ changes only parameter $j$ and $h$ is a small step. The
same local idea underlies the numerical gradient used when an analytic gradient
is unavailable.

The objects in the code correspond to the model as follows:

| Code | Model quantity |
|---|---|
| `design %*% beta` | $\eta_i$ |
| `lower` | $\kappa_0$ |
| `lower + exp(gap)` | $\kappa_1>\kappa_0$ |
| `exp(log_precision)` | $\phi>0$ |
| `p_zero`, `p_middle`, `p_one` | $p_{0i},p_{mi},p_{1i}$ |
| `dbeta(..., log=TRUE)` | interior conditional density |

```{r}
#| label: fit-ordered-beta
#| echo: true
ordered_beta_nll <- function(parameters, y, design) {
  p <- ncol(design)
  beta <- parameters[seq_len(p)]
  lower <- parameters[[p + 1L]]
  upper <- lower + exp(parameters[[p + 2L]])
  precision <- exp(parameters[[p + 3L]])
  eta <- drop(design %*% beta)
  log_p_zero <- plogis(lower - eta, log.p = TRUE)
  log_p_one <- plogis(eta - upper, log.p = TRUE)
  log_F_upper <- plogis(upper - eta, log.p = TRUE)
  log_F_lower <- plogis(lower - eta, log.p = TRUE)
  log_one_minus_exp <- function(x) {
    ifelse(
      x < log(0.5),
      log1p(-exp(x)),
      log(-expm1(x))
    )
  }
  log_p_middle <-
    log_F_upper + log_one_minus_exp(log_F_lower - log_F_upper)
  mu <- plogis(eta)
  log_likelihood <- numeric(length(y))
  is_zero <- y == 0
  is_one <- y == 1
  interior <- !is_zero & !is_one
  log_likelihood[is_zero] <- log_p_zero[is_zero]
  log_likelihood[is_one] <- log_p_one[is_one]
  log_likelihood[interior] <- log_p_middle[interior] +
    dbeta(y[interior], mu[interior] * precision,
          (1 - mu[interior]) * precision, log = TRUE)
  -sum(log_likelihood)
}
ordered_beta_gradient <- function(parameters, y, design) {
  p <- ncol(design)
  beta <- parameters[seq_len(p)]
  lower <- parameters[[p + 1L]]
  log_gap <- parameters[[p + 2L]]
  gap <- exp(log_gap)
  upper <- lower + gap
  precision <- exp(parameters[[p + 3L]])
  eta <- drop(design %*% beta)
  mu <- plogis(eta)

  score_eta <- score_lower <- score_upper <- score_precision <-
    numeric(length(y))
  is_zero <- y == 0
  is_one <- y == 1
  interior <- !is_zero & !is_one

  score_eta[is_zero] <- -plogis(eta[is_zero] - lower)
  score_lower[is_zero] <- plogis(eta[is_zero] - lower)
  score_eta[is_one] <- plogis(upper - eta[is_one])
  score_upper[is_one] <- -plogis(upper - eta[is_one])

  if (any(interior)) {
    eta_i <- eta[interior]
    mu_i <- mu[interior]
    y_i <- y[interior]
    F_lower <- plogis(lower - eta_i)
    F_upper <- plogis(upper - eta_i)
    f_lower <- dlogis(lower - eta_i)
    f_upper <- dlogis(upper - eta_i)
    p_middle <- F_upper - F_lower
    alpha <- mu_i * precision
    beta_shape <- (1 - mu_i) * precision

    score_eta[interior] <-
      (f_lower - f_upper) / p_middle +
      mu_i * (1 - mu_i) * precision *
      (-digamma(alpha) + digamma(beta_shape) +
         log(y_i) - log1p(-y_i))
    score_lower[interior] <- -f_lower / p_middle
    score_upper[interior] <- f_upper / p_middle
    score_precision[interior] <-
      digamma(precision) -
      mu_i * digamma(alpha) -
      (1 - mu_i) * digamma(beta_shape) +
      mu_i * log(y_i) +
      (1 - mu_i) * log1p(-y_i)
  }

  score <- c(
    drop(crossprod(design, score_eta)),
    sum(score_lower + score_upper),
    gap * sum(score_upper),
    precision * sum(score_precision)
  )
  -score
}
fit_response <- function(y) {
  start <- c(qlogis(mean(y)), rep(0, ncol(X) - 1L),
             qlogis(mean(y == 0) + .01), log(3), log(5)) # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  first_fit <- optim(
    start,
    ordered_beta_nll,
    y = y,
    design = X,
    method = "BFGS",
    gr = ordered_beta_gradient,
    control = list(maxit = 3000L, reltol = 1e-10)
  )
  refined_fit <- optim(
    first_fit$par,
    ordered_beta_nll,
    gr = ordered_beta_gradient,
    y = y,
    design = X,
    method = "BFGS",
    control = list(maxit = 10000L, reltol = 1e-13)
  )
  current <- refined_fit$par
  for (newton_step in seq_len(4L)) {
    current_gradient <- ordered_beta_gradient(current, y, X)
    current_hessian <- numDeriv::jacobian(
      function(par) ordered_beta_gradient(par, y, X),
      current,
      method = "Richardson"
    )
    current_hessian <- (current_hessian + t(current_hessian)) / 2
    current <- current - drop(solve(current_hessian, current_gradient))
  }
  final_hessian <- numDeriv::jacobian(
    function(par) ordered_beta_gradient(par, y, X),
    current,
    method = "Richardson"
  )
  final_hessian <- (final_hessian + t(final_hessian)) / 2
  list(
    par = current,
    value = ordered_beta_nll(current, y, X),
    convergence = refined_fit$convergence,
    hessian = final_hessian
  )
}
neg_fit <- fit_response(mnr$negraising)
ease_fit <- fit_response(mnr$acceptability)
stopifnot(neg_fit$convergence == 0L, ease_fit$convergence == 0L)
data.frame(response = c("neg-raising", "ease"),
           negative_log_likelihood = c(neg_fit$value, ease_fit$value))
```

## Fitted contributions for two observed rows

The symbolic likelihood becomes easier to read when one fitted predictor cell is carried through every region. The code below finds an actual zero and an actual interior neg-raising response with the same voice and subject, then uses the fitted parameter vector to compute their shared $\eta_i$, region probabilities, interior mean, and likelihood contributions.

```{r}
#| label: ordered-beta-one-contribution
p <- ncol(X)
beta <- neg_fit$par[seq_len(p)]
lower <- neg_fit$par[[p + 1L]]
upper <- lower + exp(neg_fit$par[[p + 2L]])
precision <- exp(neg_fit$par[[p + 3L]])

candidate_cells <- interaction(mnr$voice, mnr$subject, drop = TRUE)
usable_cell <- names(which(vapply(
  split(mnr$negraising, candidate_cells),
  function(values) any(values == 0) && any(values > 0 & values < 1),
  logical(1)
)))[[1L]]
cell_rows <- which(candidate_cells == usable_cell)
zero_row <- cell_rows[which(mnr$negraising[cell_rows] == 0)[[1L]]]
interior_row <- cell_rows[
  which(mnr$negraising[cell_rows] > 0 & mnr$negraising[cell_rows] < 1)[[1L]]
]

eta <- drop(X[zero_row, , drop = FALSE] %*% beta)
p_zero <- plogis(lower - eta)
p_one <- plogis(eta - upper)
p_middle <- 1 - p_zero - p_one # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
mu <- plogis(eta)
interior_y <- mnr$negraising[[interior_row]]

worked_contributions <- data.frame(
  observed_region = c("exact zero", "interior"),
  observed_y = c(0, interior_y),
  eta = eta,
  p_zero = p_zero,
  p_middle = p_middle,
  p_one = p_one,
  interior_mean = mu,
  likelihood_contribution = c(
    p_zero,
    p_middle * dbeta(
      interior_y,
      mu * precision,
      (1 - mu) * precision
    )
  )
)
worked_contributions
```

The exact zero contributes only $p_{0i}$. The interior response uses the same $\eta_i$ twice: once through $p_{mi}$, which determines whether the response enters the interior, and again through $\mu_i$, which locates its beta density within that region.

A comparison between two predictor cells actually represented in the data shows how the shared location assumption moves all four quantities together:

```{r}
#| label: ordered-beta-location-shift
observed_conditions <- unique(mnr[c("voice", "subject")])[1:2, ]
observed_condition_design <- model.matrix(~ voice * subject, observed_conditions)
observed_condition_eta <- drop(observed_condition_design %*% beta)
do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(observed_conditions)), function(i) {
  current_eta <- observed_condition_eta[[i]]
  current_zero <- plogis(lower - current_eta)
  current_one <- plogis(current_eta - upper)
  data.frame(
    observed_conditions[i, ],
    eta = current_eta,
    p_zero = current_zero,
    p_middle = 1 - current_zero - current_one, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
    p_one = current_one,
    interior_mean = plogis(current_eta)
  )
}))
```

The starting values place the intercept at the logit of the overall response
mean, including the endpoint observations, initialize contrasts at zero, set a
finite ordered gap, and set moderate precision. They start the numerical search
and carry no prior probability. Stable logistic CDF and log difference
calculations keep the numerical objective equal to the displayed likelihood
when a region probability is extremely small.

The optimizer reports convergence, but a return code alone is not enough. To
check the gradient independently, we move one parameter a small distance above
and below its fitted value. The change in the criterion divided by the total
step approximates that parameter's derivative; this is a **central finite
difference**. We want every such derivative to be near zero. We also inspect
the Hessian. An **eigenvector** gives a coefficient-space direction whose
direction is preserved by the curvature transformation, and its **eigenvalue**
records the curvature in that direction. A positive smallest eigenvalue is
consistent with a strict local minimum of the negative log likelihood.

```{r}
#| label: check-ordered-beta-optimum
check_ordered_beta_fit <- function(fit, y, design, response_name) {
  analytic_gradient <- ordered_beta_gradient(fit$par, y, design)
  gradient <- numDeriv::grad(
    ordered_beta_nll,
    fit$par,
    y = y,
    design = design,
    method = "Richardson"
  )
  independent_hessian <- optimHess(
    fit$par,
    ordered_beta_nll,
    y = y,
    design = design
  )
  eigenvalues <- eigen(
    independent_hessian,
    symmetric = TRUE,
    only.values = TRUE
  )$values
  covariance <- solve(independent_hessian)

  list(
    check = data.frame(
      response = response_name,
      maximum_absolute_analytic_gradient = max(abs(analytic_gradient)),
      maximum_absolute_gradient = max(abs(gradient)),
      maximum_gradient_difference = max(abs(
        analytic_gradient - gradient
      )),
      minimum_hessian_eigenvalue = min(eigenvalues),
      maximum_hessian_difference = max(abs(
        independent_hessian - fit$hessian
      )),
      maximum_relative_hessian_difference = max(abs(
        independent_hessian - fit$hessian
      )) / max(abs(independent_hessian))
    ),
    standard_errors = sqrt(diag(covariance))
  )
}

neg_check <- check_ordered_beta_fit(
  neg_fit,
  mnr$negraising,
  X,
  "neg-raising"
)
ease_check <- check_ordered_beta_fit(
  ease_fit,
  mnr$acceptability,
  X,
  "ease"
)
ordered_beta_checks <- rbind(neg_check$check, ease_check$check)
ordered_beta_checks

parameter_names <- c(
  colnames(X),
  "lower cutpoint",
  "log cutpoint gap",
  "log precision"
)
local_curvature_standard_errors <- rbind(
  data.frame(
    response = "neg-raising",
    parameter = parameter_names,
    local_standard_error = neg_check$standard_errors
  ),
  data.frame(
    response = "ease",
    parameter = parameter_names,
    local_standard_error = ease_check$standard_errors
  )
)
local_curvature_standard_errors

stopifnot(
  max(ordered_beta_checks$maximum_absolute_analytic_gradient) < 1e-7,
  max(ordered_beta_checks$maximum_absolute_gradient) < 1e-4,
  max(ordered_beta_checks$maximum_gradient_difference) < 1e-4,
  min(ordered_beta_checks$minimum_hessian_eigenvalue) > 0,
  max(ordered_beta_checks$maximum_relative_hessian_difference) < 1e-5
)
```

The independent gradient begins with symmetric finite differences and uses
Richardson extrapolation: it repeats the calculation with smaller values of
$h$ and combines the results to cancel the leading approximation error. Its
largest discrepancy from the analytic score is below $10^{-4}$. The
second Hessian calculation starts from the fitted parameters and
re-differentiates the objective independently of the Hessian stored by
`optim()`. Their largest entrywise discrepancy is less than $10^{-5}$ of the
largest curvature entry. Both analytic score vectors have every entry below
$10^{-7}$ in absolute value, and the independent numerical approximations have
every entry below $10^{-4}$. The curvature is positive in every parameter
direction.

Inverting that curvature gives the displayed local covariance approximation
under the row-independence model. The same participants and verbs recur in the
data, so we use those standard errors only to diagnose the fitted objective. The
analysis below treats the coefficients as point estimates. Population
uncertainty would require a grouped model that represents the repeated units.

```{r}
#| label: ordered-beta-raw-and-fit
#| echo: true
grid <- expand.grid(voice = levels(mnr$voice), subject = levels(mnr$subject))
X_grid <- model.matrix(~ voice * subject, grid)
eta_grid <- drop(X_grid %*% beta)
bins <- c("0", paste0(seq(.05, .95, by = .1)), "1") # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
mnr$bin <- cut(mnr$negraising,
  breaks = c(-Inf, 0, seq(.1, .9, by = .1), 1, Inf), labels = bins, # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  include.lowest = TRUE)
mnr$bin[mnr$negraising == 0] <- "0"
mnr$bin[mnr$negraising == 1] <- "1"
raw <- as.data.frame(table(mnr$voice, mnr$subject, mnr$bin,
                           dnn = c("voice", "subject", "bin")))
names(raw)[[4L]] <- "observations"
raw$empirical <- ave(raw$observations, raw$voice, raw$subject,
                     FUN = function(x) x / sum(x))
fitted_bins <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_len(nrow(grid)), function(i) {
  eta <- eta_grid[[i]]
  p0 <- plogis(lower - eta); p1 <- plogis(eta - upper)
  pm <- 1 - p0 - p1; mu <- plogis(eta)
  lo <- seq(0, .9, by = .1); hi <- seq(.1, 1, by = .1)
  interior <- pm * (pbeta(hi, mu * precision, (1 - mu) * precision) -
                      pbeta(lo, mu * precision, (1 - mu) * precision))
  data.frame(grid[i, ], bin = bins, fitted = c(p0, interior, p1))
}))
display <- merge(raw, fitted_bins, by = c("voice", "subject", "bin"))
display$bin <- factor(display$bin, levels = bins)
```

The ten interior bins are a display choice. They do not enter the likelihood, which uses each interior slider value directly through the beta density.

```{r}
#| label: plot-ordered-beta
#| echo: true
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(display, aes(bin, group = subject)) +
  geom_point(aes(y = empirical, shape = subject), size = 1.7,
             position = position_dodge(width = .18)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fitted, linetype = subject), color = "#1F5A85",
            linewidth = .65, position = position_dodge(width = .18)) +
  scale_x_discrete(breaks = c("0", ".25", ".45", ".65", ".85", "1")) + # dqr-allow: algorithm-setting
  facet_wrap(~ voice) +
  labs(x = "Neg-raising response (interior binned)", y = "Probability",
       shape = NULL, linetype = NULL) + theme_classic()
```

The fitted passive coefficient is `r round(beta[[which(colnames(X) == "voicepassive")]], 3)`, a shift on the ordered location scale. We interpret that shift through the full predictive distribution above because the coefficient alone does not say how probability moves among zero, the interior, and one.

These are fixed population fits. They omit participant and verb dependence and do not reproduce An and White's latent model weighted by acceptability. Ease remains a companion response and never filters individual trials. The ordering also assumes that predictors move endpoint use and interior location through one latent dimension; discrepancies by condition in the plot provide the relevant check.

## Recap and check your understanding

1. Which likelihood factor is used for an exact zero?
2. Why does the beta density alone not handle exact endpoints?
3. What substantive restriction is imposed by using the same $\eta_i$ for endpoint use and interior location?
4. Does changing the plotting bins change the maximum likelihood estimate?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. An exact zero contributes the lower endpoint mass $F(\kappa_0-\eta_i)$. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
2. A continuous beta distribution assigns probability zero to any exact point and has support only on the open interval. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
3. Predictors must move both endpoint probabilities and the interior beta mean along one ordered location dimension. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->
4. No. Bins summarize fitted and empirical distributions for display; the likelihood uses unbinned responses. <!-- dqr-allow: conceptual-answer -->

</details>

Having specified these generalized response models, we can ask how their restrictions perform on observations that did not determine them. This is the problem of [prediction and model criticism](../model-criticism-and-prediction/index.qmd).
